Name: Blood-Dyed Honor of the Mediterranean: The Phoenician Method of Extracting Murex Purple
RagShortTexts: Tyre and Carthage monopolized the extraction of the extremely costly royal murex purple from the hypobranchial gland of the dye murex
Ten thousand murex shells yield only one gram of pure dye; the dyed wool never fades and grows brighter the more it is exposed to the sun
The murex-purple toga was the supreme mark of honor for a triumphant Roman consul and for Phoenician princes
BaseText: 'Tyrian Purple' (also called royal murex purple) was the most noble and luxurious material symbol of the classical Mediterranean world. Relying on the traditional secret methods they monopolized, Carthage and the Phoenician ports sent slave divers to gather the marine dye murex (Murex). In open-air workshops on the shore, craftsmen cracked the shells, removed the tiny amount of pale yellow, transparent mucus from the hypobranchial gland, and placed it in great lead cauldrons with sea salt and plant ash to steep and simmer for ten days and nights. The process gave off a nauseating stench of rotting fish, but the wool fabric it dyed never faded under fierce sun and weathering; instead it turned from red to deep purple and grew ever more brilliant. One pound of fine purple-dyed wool was worth its own weight in silver. In Rome, only a commander of outstanding military merit celebrating a triumph and the highest magistrates were entitled to wear such purple robes, and it became the color of power that ruled the classical world.

Variants.Content: Only the blood of ten thousand murex shells can dye the splendor of half a bolt of noble robe! The princes and nobles of the whole Mediterranean beg for this purple glow from the Carthaginian shore with chests of silver.
The purple-bordered toga stands for the sacred, inviolable imperium of the Senate. When a consul in murex purple walks into the Forum, every barbarian who lives by violence must bow before Roman law!

We labor beside the lead cauldrons on the stinking shore until our eyes are smoked blind and our skin rots, while the rich, wrapped in purple robes soaked in our misery, hold forth from their ivory chairs.
